title: Nepal's First Woman Helicopter Captain Flies 100 Rescue Missions in Under a Week
excerpt: Captain Priya Adhikari, 40, has been flying nearly continuously over Nepal's flood-ravaged Rasuwa district, pulling survivors from mudslides that have killed more than 1,000 people across Nepal and Tibet.
body:
• Captain Priya Adhikari, 40, Nepal's first woman helicopter captain, has flown roughly 100 rescue missions in less than a week as floods and mudslides devastate the country.
  • She has been flying over Timure village in Rasuwa district, where around 20 helicopters are coordinating evacuations in thick mud with engines running through every landing.
  • An Everest rescue specialist who has flown at altitudes up to 6,200 metres, Adhikari overcame years of scepticism about women in high-altitude aviation to become a full-time pilot in 2017.
  • More than 1,000 people have been killed across Nepal and Tibet, and Adhikari says the devastation surpasses Nepal's 2015 earthquake.

When Captain Priya Adhikari lifts her helicopter from a mudslide-ravaged landing zone in Nepal's Rasuwa district, she does not know whether the ground will still be there when she returns. In the past week, the 40-year-old has flown approximately 100 rescue missions through some of the worst flood-hit terrain in the country's recent history — and she has not stopped.

Flying into the Disaster

Since devastating floods and mudslides swept across Nepal and the Tibetan Autonomous Region in late August 2026, killing more than 1,000 people, Adhikari has been airborne almost continuously above Timure village in Rasuwa district, northwest of Kathmandu. Around 20 helicopters are involved in the rescue operations, with five or six sometimes landing at the same site simultaneously, their crews coordinating constantly over the radio.

The conditions are extreme. Thick mud has made landing zones unpredictable, forcing pilots to keep their helicopters powered throughout every stop — a precaution against sinking rotors and blocked landing gear. Scores of people remain missing in the region.

"Most of us are so exhausted because of all the flights we've been doing. We've been trained for this."

— Captain Priya Adhikari, speaking to CNN's Anderson Cooper

Adhikari told CNN the scale of destruction exceeds even the 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people. "They are not my relatives," she said of the survivors and bodies she sees from the cockpit. "But when you see people and bodies from above, you carry those emotions with you."

From Cabin Crew to Cockpit

Adhikari's path to the pilot's seat was anything but direct. After studying environmental science, she spent five years working as cabin crew for a Nepali airline. A helicopter joyride — the kind sold to tourists visiting mountain valleys — changed her trajectory. She pursued flight training in the Philippines and returned to Nepal, joining Shree Airlines and becoming a full-time helicopter pilot in 2017.

She went on to become Nepal's first woman helicopter captain, a milestone achieved despite persistent scepticism about women operating aircraft solo in the country's male-dominated aviation sector. Early in her career, she faced questions about whether a woman could handle the physical demands and spatial challenges of high-altitude helicopter operations.

She answered those questions on Mount Everest. Adhikari specialises in high-altitude rescue operations and has pulled injured climbers from altitudes of up to approximately 6,200 metres — thin-air conditions where helicopter performance margins narrow dramatically and pilots must calculate weight, wind, and oxygen with precision.

Exhaustion and Resolve

The current disaster has tested even her experience. Nepal's monsoon floods in 2026 have been among the most destructive in recent decades, with torrential rains triggering landslides that buried villages and cut off roads in mountainous districts. Helicopter rescue has become the only viable access to many communities.

Adhikari and her fellow pilots have been working in shifts, but the volume of missions — and the emotional toll of what they witness — has pushed crews to their limits. The coordination challenge is as much about endurance as skill: days of continuous flying in uncertain weather, landing in compromised zones, and the constant radio negotiation of airspace shared by multiple helicopters.

Yet for Adhikari, the work carries its own reward. "Every time I go and land, I see people around and waving at them," she told CNN. "I say, you survived."

A Barrier-Breaking Career

Adhikari's story extends beyond this disaster. As the first woman to fly solo helicopter rescue missions in Nepal, she has expanded what the country's aviation sector considers possible. Her career has been cited as an example across South Asia of what women can achieve in fields long closed to them — not through symbolic appointments, but through thousands of hours of flight time in some of the world's most demanding terrain.

Now, with Nepal's flood response still ongoing and casualties likely to rise, Adhikari continues to fly. The rescue work, she said, is what she trained for — and what she will keep doing as long as there are survivors to reach.
